{{short description|Equation for the propagation of sound waves through a medium}}
{{More citations needed|date=February 2019}}

In [[physics]], the '''acoustic wave equation''' is a second-order [[partial differential equation]] that governs the propagation of [[acoustic wave]]s through a [[Transmission medium|material medium]] resp. a [[standing wave]]field.  The equation describes the evolution of [[acoustic pressure]] {{mvar|p}} or [[particle velocity]] {{mvar|'''u'''}} as a function of position {{mvar|'''x'''}} and time {{mvar|t}}. A simplified (scalar) form of the equation describes acoustic waves in only one spatial dimension, while a more general form describes waves in three dimensions.
  
For lossy media, more intricate models need to be applied in order to take into account frequency-dependent attenuation and [[Phase velocity|phase speed]]. Such models include acoustic wave equations that incorporate [[fractional derivative]] terms, see also the [[acoustic attenuation]] article or the survey paper.<ref name="Nasholm2">S. P. Näsholm and S. Holm, "On a Fractional Zener Elastic Wave Equation," Fract. Calc. Appl. Anal. Vol. 16, No 1 (2013), pp. 26-50, DOI: 10.2478/s13540-013--0003-1 [https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.4024 Link to e-print]</ref>

== Definition in one dimension==

The [[wave equation]] describing a standing wave field in one dimension (position <math>x</math>) is

<math display="block"> p_{xx} - \frac{1}{c^2} p_{tt} =0,</math>

where <math>p</math> is the [[acoustic pressure]] (the local deviation from the [[ambient pressure]]) and <math>c</math> the [[speed of sound]], using [[Notation_for_differentiation#Partial_derivatives|subscript notation]] for the partial derivatives.<ref>[[Richard Feynman]], Lectures in Physics, Volume 1, Chapter 47: [https://feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/I_47.html Sound. The wave equation], Caltech 1963, 2006, 2013</ref>

===Derivation===
{{see also|Euler equations (fluid dynamics)#Euler equations}}
Start with the [[ideal gas law]]
:<math>P = \rho R_\text{specific}T,</math>
where <math>T</math> the [[Thermodynamic temperature|absolute temperature]] of the gas and [[Gas constant#Specific gas constant|specific gas constant]] <math>R_\text{specific}</math>.
Then, assuming the process is [[adiabatic process|adiabatic]], pressure <math>P(\rho)</math> can be considered a function of density <math>\rho</math>.

[[File:Derivação da equação da onda acústica.png|400px|thumbnail|Derivation of the acoustic wave equation]]

The '''[[conservation of mass]]''' and '''[[Cauchy momentum equation|conservation of momentum]]''' can be written as a closed system of two equations{{sfn | LeVeque | 2002 | p=26}}
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\rho_{t} + (\rho u)_{x} &= 0,\\
(\rho u)_{t} + (\rho u^2 + P(\rho))_{x} &=0.
\end{align}
</math>
This coupled system of two nonlinear conservation laws can be written in vector form as:
<math display="block">q_t + f(q)_x = 0, </math>
with
<math display="block"> q = \begin{bmatrix}\rho \\ \rho u\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}q_{(1)} \\ q_{(2)}\end{bmatrix}, \quad f(q) = \begin{bmatrix}\rho u \\ \rho u^2 + P(\rho)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} q_{(2)} \\ q_{(2)}^2/q_{(1)} + P(q_{(1)})\end{bmatrix}.</math> 

To linearize this equation, let{{sfn | LeVeque | 2002 | pp=27-28}}
<math display="block">q(x,t) = q_0 + \tilde{q}(x,t),</math>
where <math>q_0 = ( \rho_0 , \rho_0 u_0)</math> is the (constant) background state and <math>\tilde{q}</math> is a sufficiently small perturbation, i.e., any powers or products of <math>\tilde{q}</math> can be discarded. Hence, the [[Taylor expansion]] of <math>f(q)</math> gives:
<math display="block">f(q_0 + \tilde{q}) \approx f(q_0) + f'(q_0)\tilde{q}</math>
where
<math display="block"> f'(q) = \begin{bmatrix} \partial f_{(1)}/\partial q_{(1)} &  \partial f_{(1)}/\partial q_{(2)}\\  \partial f_{(2)}/\partial q_{(1)} & \partial f_{(2)}/\partial q_{(2)} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -u^2 + P'(\rho) & 2u\end{bmatrix}.</math> 
This results in the linearized equation
<math display="block">\tilde{q}_t + f'(q_0)\tilde{q}_x = 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \begin{align}
\tilde{\rho}_{t} + (\widetilde{\rho u})_{x} &= 0\\
(\widetilde{\rho u})_{t} + (-u_{0}^2 + P'(\rho_{0}))\tilde{\rho }_{x} + 2u_{0}(\widetilde{\rho u})_x &=0
\end{align}</math>
Likewise, small perturbations of the components of <math>q</math> can be rewritten as:
<math display="block">\rho u = (\rho_0 +\tilde{\rho})(u_0 +\tilde{u}) = \rho_0 u_0 + \tilde{\rho}u_0 + \rho_0 \tilde{u} + \tilde{\rho}\tilde{u}</math>
such that
<math display="block">\widetilde{\rho u} \approx \tilde{\rho}u_0 + \rho_0 \tilde{u},</math>
and pressure perturbations relate to density perturbations as:
<math display="block">p = p_{0} + \tilde{p}= P(\rho_0 + \tilde{\rho}) = P(\rho_{0}) + P'(\rho_{0})\tilde{\rho} + \dots</math>
such that:
<math display="block">p_0 = P(\rho_0), \quad \tilde{p}\approx P'(\rho_0)\tilde{\rho},</math> 
where <math>P'(\rho_0)</math> is a constant, resulting in the alternative form of the linear acoustics equations:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\tilde{p}_{t} + u_0 \tilde{p}_x + K_0 \tilde{u}_x &= 0,\\
\rho_0\tilde{u}_t + \tilde{p}_x + \rho_0 u_0 \tilde{u}_x &=0.
\end{align}</math>
where <math>K_0 = \rho_0 P'(\rho_0)</math> is the [[bulk modulus]] of compressibility. After dropping the tilde for convenience, the linear first order system can be written as:
<math display="block">\begin{bmatrix}
p\\
u
\end{bmatrix}_{t} + \begin{bmatrix}
u_{0} & K_0\\
1/\rho_0 & u_0
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}
p\\
u
\end{bmatrix}_{x}=0.</math>
While, in general, a non-zero background velocity is possible (e.g. when studying the sound propagation in a constant-strength wind), it will be assumed that <math>u_{0}=0</math>. Then the linear system reduces to the second-order wave equation:
<math display="block">p_{tt} = -K_0 u_{xt} = -K_0 u_{tx} = K_0\left(\frac{1}{\rho_0}p_x\right)_x = c_{0}^2 p_{xx},</math>
with <math>c_0 = \sqrt{K_0/\rho_0}</math> the [[speed of sound]]. 

Hence, the acoustic equation can be derived from a system of first-order 
[[advection equation]]s that follow directly from physics, i.e., the [[first integral]]s:
<math display="block">q_t + Aq_x = 0,</math>
with
<math display="block">
q = \begin{bmatrix}p\\ u\end{bmatrix}, \quad A =  \begin{bmatrix}
0 & K_0\\
1/\rho_0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.</math>
Conversely, given the second-order equation <math>p_{tt} =c_{0}^2 p_{xx}</math> a first-order system can be derived:
<math display="block">q_t + \hat{A}q_x = 0,</math>
with
<math display="block">
q = \begin{bmatrix}p_t\\ -p_x\end{bmatrix}, \quad \hat{A} =  \begin{bmatrix}
0 & c_{0}^2\\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix},</math>
where matrix <math>A</math> and <math>\hat{A}</math> are [[Matrix_similarity|similar]].{{sfn | LeVeque | 2002 | p=33}}

===Solution===

Provided that the speed <math>c</math> is a constant, not dependent on frequency (the dispersionless case), then the most general solution is

:<math>p = f(c t - x) + g(c t + x)</math>

where <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are any two twice-differentiable functions. This may be pictured as the [[Superposition principle|superposition]] of two waveforms of arbitrary profile, one (<math>f</math>) traveling up the x-axis and the other (<math>g</math>) down the x-axis at the speed <math>c</math>. The particular case of a sinusoidal wave traveling in one direction is obtained by choosing either <math>f</math> or <math>g</math> to be a sinusoid, and the other to be zero, giving

:<math>p=p_0 \sin(\omega t \mp kx)</math>.

where <math>\omega</math> is the [[angular frequency]] of the wave and <math>k</math> is its [[wave number]].

==In three dimensions==

=== Equation ===

Feynman<ref name = "Feynman 1">[[Richard Feynman]], Lectures in Physics, Volume 1, 1969, Addison Publishing Company, Addison</ref> provides a derivation of the wave equation for sound in three dimensions as

:<math> \nabla ^2 p - {1 \over c^2} { \partial^2 p  \over  \partial t ^2 } = 0, </math>

where <math>\nabla ^2</math> is the [[Laplace operator]], <math>p</math> is the [[acoustic pressure]] (the local deviation from the ambient pressure), and <math>c</math> is the [[speed of sound]].

A similar looking wave equation but for the [[vector field]] [[particle velocity]] is given by
:<math> \nabla ^2 \mathbf{u}\; - {1 \over c^2} { \partial^2 \mathbf{u}\; \over  \partial t ^2 } = 0  </math>.

In some situations, it is more convenient to solve the wave equation for an abstract [[scalar field]] [[velocity potential]] which has the form 
:<math> \nabla ^2 \Phi - {1 \over c^2} { \partial^2 \Phi  \over  \partial t ^2 } = 0  </math>
and then derive the [[Physical quantity|physical quantities]] particle velocity and acoustic pressure by the equations (or definition, in the case of particle velocity):
: <math> \mathbf{u} = \nabla \Phi\;</math>,
: <math> p = -\rho {\partial \over \partial t}\Phi </math>.

===Solution===

The following solutions are obtained by [[separation of variables#Partial differential equations|separation of variables]] in different coordinate systems. They are [[phasor (sine waves)|phasor]] solutions, that is they have an implicit time-dependence factor of <math>e^{i\omega t}</math> where <math>\omega = 2 \pi f</math> is the [[angular frequency]]. The explicit time dependence is given by
:<math>p(r,t,k) = \operatorname{Real}\left[p(r,k) e^{i\omega t}\right]</math>
Here <math> k = \omega/c \ </math> is the [[wave number]].

====Cartesian coordinates====

: <math>p(r,k)=Ae^{\pm ikr} </math>.

====Cylindrical coordinates====

: <math>p(r,k)=AH_0^{(1)}(kr) + \ BH_0^{(2)}(kr)</math>.

where the asymptotic approximations to the [[Hankel function]]s, when <math>kr\rightarrow \infty </math>, are

:<math> H_0^{(1)}(kr) \simeq \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi kr}}e^{i(kr-\pi/4)}</math>

:<math> H_0^{(2)}(kr) \simeq \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi kr}}e^{-i(kr-\pi/4)}</math>.

====Spherical coordinates====

: <math>p(r,k)=\frac{A}{r}e^{\pm ikr}</math>.

Depending on the chosen Fourier convention, one of these represents an outward travelling wave and the other a nonphysical inward travelling wave.  The inward travelling solution wave is only nonphysical because of the singularity that occurs at r=0; inward travelling waves do exist.
